# reprokit

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/dm-k1/reprokit/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dm-k1/reprokit/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

> Sharing raw data remains the standard. When sharing is genuinely impossible,
> reprokit says what the minimum is that authors owe their readers, and what
> those readers lose.

reprokit works in two directions, using the same statistics.

* **Share.** If you cannot share your raw data, reprokit tells you whether
  summary statistics are enough for readers to reproduce your result exactly,
  stores those statistics, and writes an appendix that lists them.
* **Check.** If you are reading a paper that reports its statistics, reprokit
  tests whether the reported numbers are consistent with each other, taking
  rounding into account.

Raw data stays the standard. `sufficient_stats()` and `appendix()` list what
readers lose by getting summaries instead. `appendix()` records the reason you
give for not sharing the raw data; without one, it says the author did not state
one, and reprokit never suggests a reason. reprokit does not make withholding data
easier to justify; it makes the minimum you owe your readers explicit.

reprokit needs R >= 4.1 and depends only on base R (`stats`, `utils`).

## Installation

reprokit is not on CRAN. Install the development version from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("dm-k1/reprokit")

# or
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("dm-k1/reprokit")
```

The vignettes are not built by default. To get them, install with:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pak::pak("dm-k1/reprokit", dependencies = TRUE, build_vignettes = TRUE)
# or
remotes::install_github("dm-k1/reprokit", build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

Then open them with `vignette("reprokit")`. Without installing, you can read
the sources on GitHub:
[reprokit.Rmd](https://github.com/dm-k1/reprokit/blob/main/vignettes/reprokit.Rmd),
[concepts.Rmd](https://github.com/dm-k1/reprokit/blob/main/vignettes/concepts.Rmd),
[validation.Rmd](https://github.com/dm-k1/reprokit/blob/main/vignettes/validation.Rmd).

## Share: you cannot share the raw data

`sufficient_stats()` says whether summaries suffice. It never errors on the
verdict, which is one of:

* `summaries_suffice`: summary statistics determine the reported results exactly.
* `synthetic_possible`: summaries do not suffice, but synthetic data could.
* `needs_raw_data`: neither works, or the groups are so small that summaries are
  almost the data.

The printed object narrates the verdict, what to publish, what readers lose, and
which group or cell a disclosure flag fired for. It stores the statistics at full
precision:

```{r}
library(reprokit)

s <- sufficient_stats(extra ~ group, data = sleep, test = "welch")
s
```

`appendix()` writes the appendix for your paper (Markdown, ready to paste). Underneath,
it reproduces the result from the stored statistics and refuses if it does not
match your analysis. `sharing_reason` is optional:

```{r}
appendix(s, choices = list(convention = "pooled"),
         sharing_reason = "Consent did not cover public sharing.")
```

### From your fitted result

You can pass the result you already have. A `t.test()` or `cor.test()` result
needs its `data`; an `lm`, `aov` or `chisq.test()` result does not. The choices
the result records (tails, confidence level, Student or Welch, continuity
correction) are read from it and marked as such.

```{r}
sufficient_stats(t.test(extra ~ group, data = sleep), data = sleep)
sufficient_stats(aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth))
sufficient_stats(chisq.test(table(mtcars$am, mtcars$vs)))$verdict
```

For a mediation, give the two regressions:
`sufficient_stats(lm(M ~ X, data = d), lm(Y ~ X + M, data = d))`.

The appendix lists the numbers APA style asks for, any further numbers a reader
needs, the analysis choices you made (tails, confidence level, which test,
which effect-size convention), the numbers a reader cannot check from these
statistics, why the raw data are not shared, what readers lose, and a
disclosure check on small groups.

## Check: you are reading a paper

Pass the reported numbers as **strings**, so the decimals count: `"2.85"`
means anything from 2.845 to 2.855.

```{r}
check_reported("welch",
               n = c("10", "10"), m = c("0.75", "2.33"), sd = c("1.79", "2.00"),
               t = "-1.86", df = "17.8", p = ".079")
```

Reading the check output:

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| First line | The numbers are consistent or inconsistent with each other. |
| Level 0 to 3 | How much could be checked: 0 nothing; 1 statistic, df and p against each other; 2 the statistic recomputed from the descriptives; 3 the whole sufficient set is reported. |
| `verified` | An output (t, df) was recomputed from more basic numbers and matches. |
| `coherent` | The number fits the others, but only as an input to a check, or through numbers derived from other numbers. |
| `inconsistent` | The number is in a relation that fails under every variant, or in relations no single analysis choice satisfies together. |
| `not checkable` | No relation of this test reaches the number. |
| `unconfirmed` | The number's relation could not be evaluated because another input is missing. |
| Missing numbers | If a number was not reported but the others constrain it, its implied range is shown. |

A set of numbers that cannot all be right is reported as inconsistent:

```{r}
check_reported("paired", n = "20", t = "2.85", df = "19", p = ".050")
```

"Inconsistent" means the numbers cannot all be correct as reported. It does not
say which number is wrong, or why: a typo, a different test, a different
rounding or a real mistake all look the same. `check_reported()` names the test
first: `"student"`, `"welch"`, `"one_sample"`, `"paired"`, `"pearson"`, `"oneway"`,
`"factorial"`, `"chisq"`, `"gof"`, `"mediation"`, `"lm"`, `"lm_simple"` or
`"lm_moderation"`.

## What it covers

Version 0.1.0 covers, for share, check and appendix alike:

* chi-squared tests of independence and goodness of fit;
* one-sample, independent-samples (Student and Welch) and paired-samples t;
* Pearson correlation;
* one-way and factorial (two-factor) between-subjects ANOVA;
* simple, multiple and moderation regression, and simple mediation.

Everything else gets a verdict only: a verdict and advice, but no stored statistics
and no check (repeated-measures ANOVA, logistic and Poisson regression, SEM, rank
tests and Spearman, standalone effect sizes, multilevel and mixed models, GEE).

`coverage_table()` lists, for each test, the numbers APA style reports, the
sufficient set, what is missing from the APA set, what can be checked and what
cannot (with the reason), and the choices you have to declare. The table below is
generated from the handler registry when this README is built, so it is the
reference, not a copy:

```{r coverage, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(coverage_table())
```

A one-way ANOVA is checked with `check_reported("oneway", ...)` (note the lowercase `f` for the
statistic): per-group n, mean and SD, plus F, both df, eta squared and p.

```{r}
check_reported("oneway", n = c("10", "10", "10"), m = c("5.03", "4.66", "5.53"),
               sd = c("0.58", "0.79", "0.44"),
               f = "4.85", df1 = "2", df2 = "27", eta2 = "0.26", p = ".016")
```

A two-factor between-subjects ANOVA is checked with `check_reported("factorial", ...)`, one effect
at a time: pass the cell n, M and SD as a x b matrices (rows are the levels of A,
columns the levels of B) and name the `effect` (`"A"`, `"B"` or `"AB"`). In an
unbalanced design the sums of squares type (III, II or I) is a choice the report
must settle; the output lists the types that fit. Partial eta squared and partial
omega squared are conventions.

```{r}
cells <- matrix(rep("10", 4), 2)
check_reported("factorial", n = cells, m = matrix(c("4.10", "5.20", "4.80", "7.40"), 2),
               sd = matrix(rep("1.50", 4), 2), effect = "A",
               f = "15.21", df1 = "1", df2 = "36", p = "< .001", eta2 = ".30")
```

A chi-squared test is checked with `check_reported("chisq", ...)` (`"gof"` for goodness of fit): pass the table as a matrix
(a vector for goodness of fit) and the reported numbers. Yates' correction is a
variant, Cramer's V a convention.

```{r}
check_reported("chisq", n = matrix(c("30", "10", "20", "40"), 2), chisq = "15.04",
               df = "1", p = ".0001", v = ".41")
```

A regression is checked with `check_reported("lm", ...)`, with one named value per
term; use `"lm_simple"` or `"lm_moderation"` for those rows. Simple mediation is
checked with `check_reported("mediation", ...)`, which checks the paths a, b, c
and c' and the indirect effect against the product of the a and b rounding
intervals. It says "not coherent" if they cannot co-occur (a bootstrap mean can
differ a little); the indirect effect's interval is not checkable.

```{r}
check_reported("lm", b = c(wt = "-3.19", hp = "-0.04"), se = c(wt = "0.64", hp = "0.01"),
               t = c(wt = "-5.00", hp = "-3.67"), df2 = "29", k = 2)
```

## Documentation

* `vignette("reprokit")`: getting started, one worked example for authors and
  one for readers.
* `vignette("concepts")`: what the terms mean (sufficient set, APA set,
  coverage level, verdicts, rounding intervals, and so on).
* `vignette("validation")`: the evidence behind the claims, and the scripts that
  produce it.

## Status and limits

reprokit is version 0.1.0, the first release, with lifecycle "experimental":
function names and output may still change. In this version:

* It checks whether reported numbers agree with each other. It does not check
  whether the analysis was appropriate, whether the data are plausible, or
  which number is wrong.
* It cannot replace the raw data. For analyses where summaries do not suffice,
  or that are outside the list above, `sufficient_stats()` says so (`synthetic_possible`
  or `needs_raw_data`) and lists the alternatives; `appendix()` refuses.
* The disclosure check flags groups, cells, categories and factor levels with
  fewer than 5 cases (the default `threshold`). It lowers the risk of
  identifying a participant; it never removes it, and passing it is not a
  guarantee of anonymity.
* The evidence for the claims is in `inst/validation/`; each script writes its
  result to `inst/validation/results/`, and `vignette("validation")` shows them.

## Reporting bugs

Please open an issue at <https://github.com/dm-k1/reprokit/issues>. A minimal
example with the reported numbers as strings helps most.

## Citation

Run `citation("reprokit")` for the citation.

## Prior art

reprokit builds on these rather than replacing them:

* [statcheck](https://github.com/MicheleNuijten/statcheck) (Nuijten and Epskamp):
  recomputes p values from reported test statistics.
* JATSdecoder `get.stats()` (Böschen): extracts statistical results from articles.
* scrutiny (Jung): error detection for reported summary statistics, including GRIM.
* rsprite2 (Wallrich): SPRITE, reconstructing possible samples from a mean and SD.
* unsum and CLOSURE (Jung): the same reconstruction, by exhaustive search.
* Nick Brown's `f_range()`: the range of F values consistent with rounded means and SDs.
* RIVETS (Brown and Heathers): a checklist for detecting problems in a study report.
* [synthpop](https://www.synthpop.org.uk/) (Nowok, Raab and Dibben): synthetic data.
* faux (DeBruine): simulating data from a specified structure.
* DataSHIELD: analysis without moving the data.
* metacheck (DeBruine, Lakens and others): automated checks of reported results.
